stories.body:
Real Madrid forward was dropped by brands for comments Chinese media generally steered clear of outlining

I t’s been a bad start to the week for the France forward Kylian Mbappé. He missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners, and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”.

The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading.

Within hours Mbappé found himself condemned online, before being unceremoniously dropped by brands , then held responsible for state television suspending the entire top Spanish league from its schedule. On Tuesday Mbappé apologised – “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China – as did La Liga, which released a statement saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans”.

Foreign brands from Mercedes to Versace and celebrities from John Cena to Katy Perry have previously been sent to the sin bin for crossing China’s political lines on Tibet, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Mbappé’s case shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains in China 50 years after his death – to the extent that most Chinese coverage of the affair does not even mention what the footballer said.

In the video, Mbappé references a meme of himself and “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, after which a composite image of Mbappé’s face on Mao’s body pops up. (Mbappé has been nicknamed “the dictator” since his time at Paris Saint-Germain, a joke referring to his perceived influence at the club.)

The football app Dongqiudi was among the first to release a statement condemning his “inappropriate remarks”, but said: “Because his comments were offensive to China and the Chinese people, we cannot translate them.”

Chinese media have reported on reactions such as the brand desertions, and the China Football Association’s lodging of a “stern protest” with Real Madrid – who on Wednesday apologised “to the Chinese people for any offence caused” – but have generally steered clear of outlining Mbappé’s precise offence.

The topic was still trending on Chinese social media on Wednesday morning, with one hashtag relating to the superstar’s apology boasting more than 600m views.

Some posts asked variations on a simple question: “What did he actually say?”

“Many netizens without a VPN are still left in the dark about why all the talk about boycotting Mbappé is actually happening,” said Manya Koetse, editor of the Eye on Digital China newsletter, on X.

Still, many expressed anger at what was characterised as disrespect for, as well as a misunderstanding of, China’s history.

“For the majority of the [Chinese] people, Mao was and is still not seen as negatively as it is believed in the west,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University.

Mao was the founding leader of modern China, but his legacy includes radical policies such as the Great Leap Forward, an industrialisation policy blamed for a famine that killed as many as 30 million people by some estimates.

The ruling Communist party (CCP) maintains Mao was a revolutionary hero, though after his death it acknowledged another extreme policy, the violent Cultural Revolution, was a “grave mistake”.

after newsletter promotion

“There has been intense tension between Mao hatred and Mao support among the Chinese themselves,” said Gao. “This tension is even more keenly felt since the economy has slowed.”

Some scholars have pointed to a resurgence of interest in Mao among younger Chinese, with a yearning for a time they regard as more idealistic and egalitarian – something the CCP is keen to keep in check.

Jennifer Pan, professor of communication at Stanford University, said the difficulty of doing independent social science surveys over the past decade meant “our understanding of what Chinese people actually think is weak”.

“Social media doesn’t fill that gap,” she said. “It’s noisy, unrepresentative, and censored … What we see is that companies, platforms, broadcasters and the foreign ministry moved together quickly. Did this follow public anger, or did this produce public anger? Either is possible, and we can’t tell which came first.”

Whichever way round, the financial cost for Mbappé is the same. His face is a common sight on Chinese buses, in subways and in online ads, and his commercial deals could be worth “as much as $30m (£22.6m) per year”, estimated Mark Dreyer, author of Sporting Superpower, a book about China’s ambitions in the sector.

However, “as soon as someone else has decided you’ve crossed the line, it’s a race to who can cut ties quickest, who can be the most patriotic”, he said. “Then you have to kiss the ring – there really is no other way if you want to stay in the market.”

Mbappé’s and La Liga’s swift apologies suggest they are trying to avoid a fate like the NBA, whose lucrative pre-season matches were shut out of China for six years after the Houston Rockets’ then general manager, Daryl Morey, voiced support for Hong Kong pro-democracy protests in 2019.

La Liga may have better luck, with the state broadcaster CCTV saying it would listen to what Mbappé had to say, and “more importantly” watch what he does.

On Wednesday a foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”

Dreyer said: “It doesn’t sound like it’s an instant: ‘All is forgiven.’ But it sounds like they’re going to be a little bit more, for want of a better word, reasonable.”

stories.title: China’s snooping around Pacific undersea cables raises risks for Big Tech
stories.summary: US-owned trans-Pacific cables face growing risks from sabotage and China.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
US-owned trans-Pacific cables face growing risks from sabotage and China.

Subsea cable projects owned by US companies such as Google and Meta face some of the greatest risks from the threat of deep-sea sabotage in the Pacific Ocean, according to a new report. That coincides with Chinese research ships spending an extraordinary amount of time apparently surveying undersea cables—not to mention Chinese commercial ships being investigated for cutting cables in both European and Asian waters.

Most damage to the undersea cables that form the Internet’s backbone is the result of accidents involving bottom-trawling fishing nets and ship anchors dragging on the seabed, with storms and undersea landslides also factoring in. But the recent rise in international tensions and open conflicts have placed new scrutiny on more suspicious instances of cable-cutting damage, with analysts warning about Russia and China in particular engaging in cable sabotage or tampering as “gray zone” tactics that fall short of direct military confrontation.

One of the newest risk assessments of China’s gray zone tactics targeting the Internet’s undersea infrastructure comes from a research report published by the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission , an independent government commission that advises Congress. The report was contracted to the London-based think tank China Strategic Risks Institute and published in September 2026.

Mapping the risks

The report authors created an interactive Trans-Pacific Cable Gray Zone Vulnerability Index that ranks the undersea cables considered most at risk and displays a map of their routes spanning the Pacific Ocean. Such an index could help identify which cables should get highest priority in terms of placing underwater sensors or setting up patrols to monitor for threats.

Risk factors used in the vulnerability index include the undersea depth of the cable routes, nearby shipping traffic, cable ownership, China’s exclusive economic zone and broader territorial claims , and whether each cable connects to Taiwan. Taiwan is considered a geopolitical hotspot as a self-governing island democracy that is also claimed by China, with the latter ramping up military maneuvers involving warships and aircraft around Taiwan in recent years.

The index suggests that the risk to cables is highest around Taiwan, Japan, and the Philippines, partly because of China’s claim of sovereignty over Taiwan but also because subsea cables linking the region to the United States must pass through shallow water with busy shipping lanes.

Among the 10 trans-Pacific cables identified as being most at risk, several are still under development with significant ownership stakes from US companies. These include the TPU project, owned by Google, the ORCA cable, owned by Meta, and the E2A cable, co-owned by Verizon along with firms in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan. All three of these projects had risk scores in the top five.

The report authors warn that any serious disruption to a single trans-Pacific cable could “risk overwhelming current available capacity on direct routings between the United States, Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines, forcing data onto slower, less direct routes.”

An even greater disruption involving multiple cables, potentially during a geopolitical crisis involving Taiwan, could “significantly reduce headroom and even overwhelm trans-Pacific capacity as a whole,” with communications between the United States and Indo-Pacific region having to reroute through other cables across the globe. That could have major economic consequences for Internet communications, cloud services, and financial trading.

Dual-use technologies and survey tracks

This comes as the world’s major powers continue to build up their fleets of military submarines and undersea drones, along with further developing and deploying dual-use technologies, like undersea cable cutters that could either be used for repair or sabotage.

China has also deployed a fleet of research vessels equipped with seabed-mapping technologies near trans-Pacific undersea cables, according to a separate report published in October 2026 by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a think tank based in Washington, DC.

The CSIS analysts found that China-flagged research ships stood out as outliers in the amount of time spent near subsea infrastructure. They analyzed the movements of more than 200 research ships from multiple nations between 2020 and 2025.

This pattern involving Chinese vessels stood out even when compared with the generally high activity of US and Russian research ships on the high seas. Several Chinese ships spent much of their time performing survey-style tracks near undersea cables rather than checking out regions known for undersea mineral deposits.

One of the most surprising findings involved the China-linked research vessel Ke Xue that made a journey to the Bering Sea between Russia and the United States. While likely checking out a US military base in the Aleutian Islands, the ship also began doing “survey-like movements” near a Russian government-owned cable called Polar Express.

That likely indicates China’s interest in mapping Russia’s subsea telecommunications infrastructure, even though China and Russia have maintained strong economic and military ties, according to the CSIS analysts.

Chinese-owned fishing boats and cargo vessels have been involved in several notable cable-cutting incidents in recent years, especially near Taiwan. One incident in 2025 led to the first case of Taiwan’s government convicting and sentencing a Chinese captain to three years in prison, after his ship dropped anchor and performed a zigzag pattern that damaged the Tai-Peng 3 cable linking Taiwan to the offshore islands of Penghu.

The broader threat

The Pacific is not the only region where undersea cables face growing danger. In recent years, both Russian- and Chinese-linked ships have been investigated for causing damage to subsea communications cables, power cables, and pipelines in the Baltic Sea. These incidents typically involved ships that dragged their anchors over unusually long periods of time.

On October 21, The Telegraph published an analysis showing more than 500 incidents involving Russia’s fleet of fishing boats loitering near crucial undersea cables connecting the UK to the rest of the world, with some vessels following the routes of the undersea cables. Reuters reporting also recently revealed that NATO countries had confronted Russian submarines that were practicing how to disable undersea cables using a new type of technology in Arctic waters near Norway earlier this year.

Meanwhile, Iran has repeatedly threatened to charge fees to US tech companies for the undersea Internet cables running beneath the contested Strait of Hormuz and has prepared plans to attack them —another consequence of the wider war that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February 2026.

For a big-picture perspective on why the world has become more dangerous for the Internet’s undersea backbone, Ars recently interviewed Elisabeth Braw , author of the book Undersea War .

This story was updated on October 28, 2026 with additional details about how a China-linked research vessel unexpectedly spent some time apparently surveying a Russian subsea cable.

stories.title: China's families are now supporting more old people than kids
stories.summary: The latest figures mark a major milestone as Beijing grapples with an ageing population.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 27 October 2026

Families in China are for the first time supporting more elderly people than children, the country's government has said.

Official data released in the last week , external show the ratio of China's dependent elderly people compared to the working age population rose to 23% last year, overtaking the figure for children, which stood at 22%.

The numbers are closely watched for signs of how China's shrinking workforce will impact both the world's second largest economy and global growth as a whole.

The latest figures mark a significant milestone as China grapples with an ageing population that could have implications for families, pensions and healthcare spending, analysts say.

China has been preparing for a growing proportion of elderly people in recent years, while urging younger generations to get married and for couples to have more children .

The latest data from China's National Bureau of Statistics show there are now more than 223 million people in China aged 65 and above, accounting for nearly 16% of the country's total population.

At the same time there are about 213 million children aged 14 and under.

No official commentary was published with the statistics. But Chinese state-controlled news outlet Global Times wrote that the nation's "entry into a moderately ageing society" is the result of a mix of factors, including the "size of past birth cohorts" and longer life expectancy.

The shift could place added strain on pension, healthcare and long-term care systems, while also creating opportunities in the so-called silver economy that caters to older consumers, the newspaper said.

"It reflects a historical trend in demographic development rather than a short-term phenomenon," Global Times quoted one researcher as saying.

The demographic shift is "symbolic" and could suggest more public spending will move from families and schools to pensions and healthcare, said Professor Stuart Gietel-Basten from The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

It may also pose a challenge to the country's ambitions, as it could limit its economic growth as well as people's spending power, said National University of Singapore sociology lecturer Mu Zheng.

Birth rates in China have been falling for years now

China's ageing population has been driven by a mix of factors, including rapid urbanisation and the effects of the controversial one-child policy , which was in place from 1980 to the end of 2015.

The strategy, designed to keep China's rapid population growth under control, is estimated by the country's government to have prevented about 400 million births since it began, though this number has been contested.

The policy played a key role in shrinking the population and means there are fewer younger people to support a growing number of elderly relatives, Mu said.

But despite easing restrictions on the size of families, Beijing has struggled to persuade couples to have more children, with birth rates hitting historic lows.

Other contributing factors include changing gender roles, rising living costs and higher education levels that have put pressure on fertility rates, Mu said.

Beijing made further support for older people a part of the measures in its five-year economic blueprint that was announced earlier this year.

Financial help for pensioners has been a growing part of Chinese government spending. More than 53 million elderly people were receiving senior citizen allowances and subsidies by the end of 2025, according to official figures.

The Global Times noted that many people entering old age who were born between the 1950s and the 1970s have generally higher incomes compared to previous generations, stronger purchasing power and are healthier.

The dependency ratio is widely-used to measure ageing populations but it has also been questioned by some experts who argue that its scope is too limited.

Gietel-Basten said the use of the statistics risks "taking agency away" from older people - many of whom he says have been misrepresented as dependants.

It also does not take into account improvements to healthcare, he added.

stories.body:
OBR outlook for living standards also downgraded as part of impact of Middle East conflict on economy

Healey offers £100 payment to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

Budget 2026 live – latest updates

Britain’s economy has taken a multibillion-pound hit as the war in the Middle East drags down growth and triggers a fresh cost of living crisis, according to the government’s independent forecaster.

In a report as John Healey announced his first budget, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) issued a sharp downgrade for growth, living standards and the public finances despite the measures taken by the chancellor .

Although Healey sought to cushion the blow through “breathing space” policies to help households and businesses with soaring energy costs, the watchdog slashed its growth forecasts for 2027 and warned that inflation was poised to reach close to 4% as Britain’s early resilience to the war fizzles out.

While growth this year was upgraded from 1.1% to 1.2% after an unexpectedly resilient performance fuelled by AI investment, the watchdog slashed its estimate for next year from 1.5% to 1%.

Highlighting the damage from Donald Trump’s war in the Gulf, Healey said the exchequer was spending £14bn more on debt interest as the financial market fallout from the conflict pushes up borrowing costs for governments worldwide.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, the chancellor said he would allow a hit to his buffer against the government’s fiscal rules – while also announcing a temporary rise in tax on banks to fund his package of energy support.

He left £15bn of headroom against the main fiscal rule , which requires day-to-day spending to be matched by tax receipts in three years’ time – down from £23.6bn left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, in the spring.

As a consequence, the OBR said borrowing was poised to fall to about 2% of GDP in the medium term but at a slower near-term pace than previous plans.

As the energy price shock rippling out from the Middle East hits households and businesses, the OBR said consumers would face inflation of 3.5% this year, significantly higher than the 2% forecast in March.

Healey made helping families with the cost of living a core focus of his first budget, including £100 in blanket payments for 20 million households at a cost to the exchequer of £2.6bn and a plan to abolish standing charges on gas bills .

Despite the measures, the OBR warned that households would come under sustained pressure, with per-person disposable incomes taking account of inflation expected to fall in the short-term before rising modestly before the end of the current parliament.

Setting the stage for a tough election run-up for Labour, the watchdog said income levels would only be about 2% above pre-pandemic levels by the start of the 2030s.

Britain’s economy had shown more resilience than had been expected at the start of the Iran war, after recording the strongest rate of growth in the G7 in the first half of 2026. Official figures suggested a strong expansion in AI-related business activity as one factor behind the surprise rise.

after newsletter promotion

Healey sought to use his budget to harness the power of the technology to boost growth in future while also safeguarding the country against the risk of cyber-attacks amid the accelerating global AI race.

Although saying he would never be complacent, Healey said there were “signs of resilience” in the economy as he highlighted that the Bank of England and the International Monetary Fund had issued growth upgrades for the UK within recent months.

“There are real challenges ahead but Britain has beaten the forecasts this year, and with the action I am taking today I believe Britain can beat the forecasts again,” he said.

However, the economy is coming under mounting pressure from the energy price shock triggered by the war. Since the start of the US-Israeli led invasion of Iran at the end of February, which has throttled energy flows in the region, oil prices have risen from about $70 a barrel to more than $115, while gas prices have almost tripled.

With a tentative pause in the fighting while Donald Trump prepares for crunch midterm elections, the OBR said the outlook for the economy, households and the UK public finances remained highly uncertain.

Suggesting there were “significantly better or worse outcomes of broadly equal probability”, it said that if energy prices were to rise to a higher and more sustained peak, government borrowing could be £17bn above the central forecast next year. However, a lower energy price path could reduce borrowing by £12bn.

stories.title: Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
stories.summary: Changes announced by Chancellor John Healey in his first Budget will affect your finances directly. Here's how.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 28 October 2026, 13:45 GMT

Families facing cost-of-living pressures are being offered some help, or "breathing space" as Chancellor John Healey is calling it.

The help comes as prices are rising faster than expected with annual energy bills in particular likely to increase by around £300 or more in January.

Here's how the key announcements in the Budget affect you and your money.

Help with your energy bill

If you are living in a home in council tax bands A to D in England, you will receive a one-off £100 "Household Energy Payment" from January, funded by extra tax on banks.

It will be paid directly into your bank account.

You can find your council tax band by looking on your annual bill, or by looking on the government's website , external - although that was struggling to cope with traffic after the announcement.

Administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive the equivalent funding, and they will decide whether to introduce the same payment.

This is designed to help with soaring energy bills, with a typical annual bill expected to be £2,000 or more in January.

The VAT cut on electricity bills, which was introduced in October, will also be extended to July. It was due to end in April.

Healey announces £100 energy payment for millions and bank tax rise in first Budget

Budget 2026: Key points at a glance Published Just now

Gas standing charges scrapped

The fee for connecting to your gas supply so called standing charges will be scrapped in England, Scotland and Wales, next year "or as soon as possible after", the chancellor said.

These fixed daily charges will then be shifted onto the price you pay for each unit of energy.

The Treasury calculates that 60% of households will save an average of £45 a year, with lower users gaining the most. But the saving will come after the projected big rise in bills in January.

Higher users - in the biggest houses but also large, low-income families - will pay more than they currently do.

The government wants to extend reforms to electricity standing charges later.

Fuel duty help if you drive

The 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel, introduced by Rishi Sunak in 2022, will be extended to July. It was scheduled to be phased out from January.

It means drivers will still pay the levy at 52.95p per litre.

Motor fuel prices have risen sharply owing to the continued impact of the Iran war on drivers, with diesel having recently hit new records when it moved above £2 per litre.

The cost of filling a typical family car with diesel has gone up by around £30 since late February. A tankful of petrol costs about £23 more.

You can still save £20,000 a year in cash tax-free

The chancellor has scrapped his predecessor's plans to reduce the annual amount people can save tax-free in cash in Individual Savings Accounts (Isas).

Rachel Reeves had wanted the policy to encourage personal investment in stocks and shares.

It meant, from April 2027, if you're under 65, you would only be able to save £12,000 a year in cash in an Isa, rather than £20,000.

But that plan has now been ditched.

Instead, the government plans to create a new "Starter Isa" for first-time investors.

You may get a pay rise

Minimum wage rates will rise by 3.9% in April. It means:

Eligible workers aged 21 and over on the National Living Wage will receive £13.21 an hour, up from £12.71

If you are aged 18, 19 or 20, the National Minimum Wage will increase to £11.27 an hour, up from £10.85

For those aged 16 or 17, the minimum wage will rise to £8.31 an hour, up from £8

The separate apprentice rate which applies to eligible people under 19 - or those over 19 in the first year of an apprenticeship – will also increase to £8.31 an hour, from £8

However, these figures mean, this time around, there's no progress on Labour's manifesto promise to narrow the gap in minimum wages between older and younger workers.

For all workers, the ongoing freeze in the income bands, or thresholds, at which income tax is paid went unmentioned in the Budget.

But it means any kind of pay rise could drag you into a higher tax bracket, or see a greater proportion of your income taxed than would otherwise be expected. Scotland has its own income tax bands.

How much is the minimum wage going up by? Published 11 minutes ago

State pension to rise

The triple lock policy means that the state pension will go up in line with average wage increases, at 3.9%.

It means:

the flat-rate state pension for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 will be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year, up £488 on now

the old basic state pension for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 will be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, up £374.40 on now

But some pensioners won't be taxed

The government had already committed to not taxing people who only get an income from the state pension.

The chancellor said this would be the case until at least 2030, as there will be a new Pension Tax Allowance, so pensioners with an income up to the value of the full new state pension will not pay income tax.

Support to save for your first home

The First Time Buyer Isa has been in the planning stages with the government for a while.

Healey has confirmed that it is intended to replace the often-criticised Lifetime Isa.

Separately, he confirmed the Your First Home equity scheme to allow first-time buyers in England to buy a new-build home with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their property's value to help pay for the purchase.

No relief if you are repaying a student loan

The government has made no changes to student loan rates - saying only that it is being "kept under review".

There has been some backlash after the previous chancellor froze the repayment threshold for Plan 2 student loans, which were given out for just over a decade in England from 2012.

It means the salary at which borrowers start paying back their loans is due to stay at £29,385 in April and remain there for three years – so graduates start repaying sooner and repay more each month than they would otherwise have done.

What else will affect your money?

Some announcements affecting your finances have already been made by the government.

They include:

Tariffs removed from 100 food items such as baked beans and garlic, which the government calculates could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June

Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030

Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period

Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that

The prime minister's plan to reinstate the £2 cap on bus fares in England from January to be in effect throughout 2027. Some cities already have caps, and funding is being given to the devolved nations

stories.title: South Carolina's measles outbreak jumped to Washington state 5 times in 2 weeks
stories.summary: International travel used to be the main risk of measles cases in the US—not anymore.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
International travel used to be the main risk of measles cases in the US—not anymore.

Since measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000, the country’s occasional cases have come mainly from international travelers—visitors from far-flung places where the virus still spreads freely—or unvaccinated US residents who return from abroad with a highly infectious souvenir. But as vaccination rates have slipped nationwide in recent years and outbreaks grow bigger and more frequent, domestic travel now poses a greater risk than international incursions.

In a study published this week in NEJM Evidence, Washington state health officials highlight that risk, detailing how an explosive outbreak in South Carolina reached their distant state through five distinct importation events over two weeks in January. In all, the introductions led to 26 cases among residents before officials stamped out the spread.

South Carolina’s measles outbreak began on October 2, 2025, and was declared over on April 26, 2026. Officials confirmed 997 cases in the state during the outbreak. At the time, it was the largest measles outbreak recorded since the virus was declared eliminated, but Pennsylvania’s ongoing outbreak has since surpassed it.

The study in Washington relied heavily on epidemiological data, linking cases among contacts and exposure sites. But also key to the work was whole-genome sequencing, which made clear that cases didn’t just stem from one single introduction of the virus from South Carolina that then spread among Washington residents; instead, it revealed five separate introductions.

“As public health jurisdictions prepare to respond to increased measles importations linked to domestic measles outbreaks, while remaining vigilant for international importations, timely whole-genome sequencing can supplement epidemiologic information to help differentiate distinct importations from local transmission and inform outbreak response,” the authors conclude.

Importations

In their analysis, health officials identified the first importation in a resident who fell ill with the telltale rash on January 12 after returning from a trip to South Carolina, where they were exposed to a person sick with measles. Genome sequencing found that the virus closely matched sequences from South Carolina cases. One close contact of the Washington case fell ill and was isolated. No other cases were linked to this importation.

In a second importation event, South Carolina residents visited public places while infectious. As a result, four residents with close contact with the South Carolina visitors fell ill. While infectious, the four residents visited schools, healthcare facilities, and a church. Nine of their contacts and one person exposed in a public location fell ill, leading to a total cluster of 14 cases that spanned January 15 to February 17.

In the third importation event, two state residents returned from South Carolina and fell ill on January 15 to 16. No additional cases were linked to these residents. Similarly, a fourth importation event occurred when a resident returned from travel. The person adhered to isolation and quarantine recommendations, and no cases were linked to this one.

In the fifth importation event, a Washington state resident returned from out-of-state travel where they had contact with ill contacts and fell ill themselves on January 19. While contagious, they visited a school and a healthcare facility. Six close contacts fell ill. In all, this cluster of seven cases spanned January 19 to January 29. The genome sequences from five of the cases were nearly identical to those seen in South Carolina.

Officials credit basic public health work of quarantines, isolation, and contact tracing with keeping the virus from spreading farther than it did.

Contradicting Kennedy

While the study highlights how readily this virus can spread among states amid declining vaccination, it also contradicts a common talking point from Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Kennedy, a prominent anti-vaccine advocate, has downplayed the current measles surge in the US and aggressively defended against suggestions that his decades of anti-vaccine misinformation and disinformation have contributed to the surge in cases and drop in vaccination.

Instead, Kennedy claims that there is a “global outbreak” and the US is “doing a better job than any country in the world at controlling the measles outbreak.” Both claims are false . Dozens of other countries have lower case rates than the US. While some countries, including neighboring Canada and Mexico, are also seeing large increases in cases, the soaring case tally in the US is not being driven by international imports, but by domestic spread in under-vaccinated communities.

According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , only 18 of the country’s 4,588 confirmed measles cases this year were reported among international visitors. Of all the cases, 4,404 (96 percent) are linked to a domestic outbreak. The US has had 43 new outbreaks this year.

Payment to 20m homes part of package to help cut energy bills and ease cost-of-living crisis, paid for by bank windfall tax

Budget 2026: key points at a glance

Budget 2026 live – latest updates

John Healey promised to steer Britain through “global economic storms,” as he announced a package of measures to cut consumers’ energy bills, funded by a smaller-than-expected windfall tax on banks.

In his first budget, the chancellor said 20m households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 payment – a measure he said would cost £2.6bn.

He extended the VAT cut on electricity bills until next July; and as widely expected, cancelled fuel duty rises pencilled in by Rachel Reeves.

Healey said this would back businesses, as well as consumers. “For millions of people, the cost of living and the cost of doing business are the same. The home is the office. The van is the family car,” he said.

Healey blamed the ongoing war in the Middle East for the deterioration in the economic outlook since Reeves’s spring statement, but insisted he would keep Labour’s deficit-reduction plans on track.

“Analysts like to speak of economic headwinds, but what we face today are global economic storms,” he said, describing his statement as “a budget built on fiscal discipline, which matches immediate action today with clear direction for the future”.

He said higher inflation as a result of the Iran war was expected to cost the government £14bn more in interest costs and the Office for Budget Responsibility had downgraded its growth forecast to 1% for next year, from the 1.6% it expected in the spring.

Nevertheless, Healey promised to meet Labour’s first fiscal rule, on balancing current spending with tax receipts by 2029-30; but with diminished headroom of £15bn – against the £24bn that Reeves set aside in March.

However, he said the cushion would be rebuilt to £22bn, by 2030-31. “That is what a buffer is for. Use it when you need it, rebuild it when you can.”

As a result of continued high oil prices caused by the Middle East conflict, the energy price cap, which determines household bills, is expected to rise sharply in January.

As well as the short-term support measures to cushion consumers against soaring prices, Healey signalled a radical reform to the way energy bills are charged in the longer term – calling it “a new cost control framework, to drive down all aspects of energy bills.”

after newsletter promotion

He said the energy package would be funded by a windfall tax on Britain’s banks – as well as an unexpected 2 percentage-point income tax rise for landlords and savers.

He said he would double the additional levy the banks pay on their profits, to 6% from the current 3%, for 15 months from January. That fell short of the rise to 8% that industry figures had expected.

Healey lavished praise on the sector, as he announced the measure. “I want to say directly to our banks: I celebrate and I am grateful for the role that you play,” he said. Bank share prices rose after the announcement, with NatWest and Standard Chartered up by more than 4%.

Healey announced several measures aimed at cutting businesses’ costs – including raising the business rates relief threshold from £12,000 to £18,000 for firms in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. He said this change would be funded by higher taxes on gambling and vape shops.

And there was a package of policies that Healey said would tackle the “moral mission” of homelessness – including cheaper borrowing for councils; VAT relief on the sale of land to social housing providers; and the confirmation of the new My First Home mortgage scheme for first-time buyers, first mooted at Labour’s party conference in September.

stories.title: Burnham insists 'no confusion at all' over his Brexit position
stories.summary: The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the Brexit deal at a summit in Brussels next month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The prime minister said he had been 'entirely consistent' on the issue

Published 28 October 2026, 13:38 GMT

Andy Burnham has insisted there is "no confusion" over his position on the European Union, as he criticised the UK's current deal with the bloc.

The prime minister said it was his "responsibility" to improve the deal, which was ratified in 2020, at a summit in Brussels next month.

He denied he had shifted his stance since the Makerfield by-election when he promised not to "re-run" the Brexit debate . Earlier this week, he suggested he could call a referendum on the UK returning to EU freedom of movement, before No10 appeared to backtrack .

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch accused him during Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday of failing to "respect" the 2016 Brexit vote.

Badenoch said Burnham had created confusion and asked if he wanted a referendum on rejoining the EU.

"There is no confusion at all," Burnham told MPs.

"The government has a collectively agreed position, which I have set out today.

"It is entirely consistent with everything that I've said, including in the by-election.

"The red lines in our manifesto, including on freedom of movement, will stay in place firmly for the whole of this Parliament."

Labour's 2024 election manifesto ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

Freedom of movement allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country.

It is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market, which enables goods, services and people to move freely between EU member states.

Badenoch accused Burnham of having "opened his mouth without engaging his brain" over freedom of movement during "the chancellor's big week" as the Budget is unveiled .

'The country was paralysed'

Recalling the mood in Parliament and the country in 2017 when the current Brexit deal was being fought over, Badenoch said: "We do not want to go through that again - the country was paralysed.

"It was miserable, regardless of which side of the debate you were on."

Burnham said Badenoch was "speaking the truth" here and the country had suffered from low growth and insufficient control on migration as a result of a "harder Brexit than what was promised" in the 2016 referendum.

"Where I am focused is getting a better deal for Britain, that is my responsibility, and I will lead from this despatch box over the next few weeks," Burnham said.

At a summit in Brussels on 20 November, Burnham will push options for a reset of relations with the bloc on issues such as youth mobility, food, drink, energy and cooperation on illegal immigration.

Video appears to show Mao Zedong called a ‘dictator’

Dongpeng and Mengniu end deals with the player

Kylian Mbappé has apologised after the Real Madrid forward was dropped by major Chinese brands for apparently joking about Mao Zedong in a video that has gone viral. There were also signs of broader repercussions, with the state-run Chinese digital newspaper The Paper reporting that public television was suspending broadcasts of matches from La Liga.

The offending video shows Mbappé saying that the funniest internet meme he had seen involving him was of his face photoshopped on to that of “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”. This was an apparent reference to a meme of Mbappé superimposed on an image of Mao.

“My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world. I apologise to everyone my words have upset,” Mbappé said in a statement in French, Chinese and English.

Spain’s La Liga also apologised, saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans. These comments were made in a personal capacity and do not represent La Liga.” In China, jokes about Mao, the country’s founding leader who died in 1976 – and whose drastic policies are also blamed by historians for mass starvation and millions of deaths – remain taboo.

The beverage giant Dongpeng, which during this year’s World Cup ran adverts with AI-generated images of Mbappé consuming its sport drink, said it was terminating all cooperation with the France captain. “Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments,” Dongpeng said in a statement.

Mengniu, China’s largest dairy producer, and cheese maker Milkground also said that they were cutting ties with Mbappé, who until now was hugely popular among Chinese fans with millions of social media followers. “Dongpeng Beverage ends cooperation with Mbappé” was the top-trending topic on Chinese social media site Weibo with 430m views.

One Weibo user said the “extremely serious wrong remarks … crossed the red line” and others urged Dongpeng to remove Mbappé’s image from their bottles. Dongqiudi, one of China’s biggest online football outlets, said Mbappé’s remarks were “offensive to China and the Chinese people”.

In an interview with the French sports newspaper L’Equipe last month, the 27-year-old Mbappé addressed a previous meme depicting him as a military dictator. “There’s a part of it that’s funny … but there is another part that’s a bit less funny because of the damage such people have caused throughout history,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry said it was aware of the reports regarding Mbappé, who on Monday finished runner-up to Harry Kane in the Ballon d’Or award for the world’s best player. “Words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with unanimous rejection from all sectors of Chinese society,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun told a regular briefing.

after newsletter promotion

The Paper cited sources at the state broadcaster saying that CCTV has suspended all broadcasts of La Liga matches, and removed all advertisements involving Mbappé. On the CCTV website, La Liga matches this weekend were still on its online viewing schedule.

Global sports stars who have commented on sensitive topics such as Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong have previously caused controversy in China and been dumped by sponsors there. The former NBA player Dwight Howard referred to Taiwan as a country in 2023 as he appeared in a video with the island’s then vice-president and current president, Lai Ching-te, sparking fury on Chinese social media. Beijing claims Taiwan is part of its territory and has threatened to use force to bring it under its control.

The Houston Rockets general manager, Daryl Morey, posted a tweet in 2019 supporting Hong Kong protests, leading to China suspending sponsorship deals with the NBA and pulling games off Chinese television for a year.

Fans in China made their feelings clear. “I used to really enjoy watching Mbappé play on the pitch,” Zhang Jingqi, 30, who works at a mall in Beijing, said. “But ever since this news broke yesterday I have lost that admiration, sorry to say.”

stories.title: Social Media When Elections Are Close: Doing the Impossible Better
stories.summary: Everyone knows, or should, that perfect (balanced, targeted, transparent, swift and swiftly appealable) content moderation at scale is impossible. That doesn’t mean powerful social platforms don’t have to try to get at least reasonably close, especially when access to good information can have a profound effect on political participation and speech. That’s why so many people, including the Meta Oversight Board , criticized Meta for suspending a major political Instagram account for hours during a huge early voting push on October 17; and for allegedly boosting one candidate in Brazil’s recent presidential election. Meta denies deliberate interference in either instance, blaming “mistakes” in its automated content moderation systems (including AI tools that can’t tell the difference between enthusiastic follower engagement and a bot attack). Mistakes or not, with early voting in the U.S. midterms already underway, these events serve as a stark reminder that all major social media platforms need to have stronger systems in place to ensure that they serve, rather than impede, democratic communication. Access to good information can have a profound effect on political participation and speech. This is not inherently an “AI” problem: automated systems can process content at a scale that humans never could, potentially enabling better moderation at scale and alleviating the psychological load on ill-paid moderators whose jobs require them to view incredibly disturbing content. But automated systems also reproduce existing biases, struggle to understand context, and often make mistakes that disproportionately affect journalists, activists, artists, and other vulnerable and marginalized communities. And moderation errors are even more likely when the language is spoken principally by the global majority. In 2020, leaked document showed that Meta’s algorithms incorrectly deleted nonviolent Arabic-language content 77 percent of the time, while failing to detect hate speech under the company’s own policies in many instances. Where these systems are faltering in Arabic, they’re positively failing in less-resourced languages. stories.title: New Records Obtained by EFF Expose More Problems with Medicare’s AI Experiment
stories.summary: New records obtained by EFF expose additional issues with Medicare’s AI-driven prior authorization program and show why we need stronger legal limits around government use of automated decision-making . EFF sued the government back in March for information about the Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction (WISeR) model , a new Medicare program that uses AI to evaluate prior authorization requests for certain medical services. We previously released records showing that WISeR has resulted in delays and denials of care, operational chaos, and reports of patient harm. Today, we’re publishing over 800 new pages of records, including: Requests for information (RFIs) or requests for corrective action plans (CAPs) sent from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to four of the six WISeR vendors, along with the vendors’ responses. Applications of 66 companies to the WISeR model, including those of the 6 selected companies. Task orders and contracts for the evaluation, implementation, and monitoring of the WISeR model. Documents obtained through EFF’s lawsuit are available here . These newly released documents show that the WISeR rollout was rushed and rocky from the start, highlighting the dangers that arise when governments treat AI like a silver bullet for complex problems. The documents also highlight the need for more transparency about safeguards against inappropriate, AI-driven denials. The public still lacks the information needed to assess whether clinician review is providing meaningful oversight of AI systems and whether appropriate data is being used to evaluate prior authorization requests. EFF has long argued that AI has no place in consequential government decisions about peoples’ rights or access to benefits, such as immigration enforcement and policing decisions. That’s because using automated decision-making in these contexts risks decisions that violate people’s rights or deprive them of benefits they’re entitled to based on biased or inappropriate considerations and without proper due process or accountability if there is an error. By outsourcing decision-making to private AI companies without sufficient transparency, testing, or legal limits, WISeR jeopardizes seniors’ access to medical care. stories.title: Mbappé sorry for 'ill-judged' Mao remark after backlash in China
stories.summary: The France star had referred to the former Chinese leader as a "dictator" during an interview about memes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A backlash has erupted on Chinese social media over Mbappé's comments on a "Chinese dictator"

Published 27 October 2026

Kylian Mbappé has apologised for "ill-judged" comments he made about late Chinese leader Mao Zedong which led to him being dropped by several Chinese brands.

Mbappé had reportedly told French talk show The Bridge the meme "that makes me laugh the most, it's the one where there's a video of a guy, I think it's a Chinese dictator..." He then laughs as the clip cuts to a meme showing his face superimposed on an image resembling Mao.

The meme is part of a running joke about the Real Madrid forward being called a "dictator" because of his huge influence in football.

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappé said in a statement.

"I apologise to everyone my words have upset."

Spain's La Liga also apologised, saying it "deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé's recent comments have caused among Chinese fans".

The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his chaotic and often violent rule that left millions dead.

A few people came out in support of him on Chinese social media, but that is a rare response given China's tightly controlled internet, where people are expected to toe the party and government line on sensitive topics.

Few topics are as sensitive as Mao, which may explain why brands were so quick to terminate partnerships with a global sports star like Mbappé.

The original video is not available on the show's YouTube channel, and it's unclear when the interview hosted by Real Madrid's Aurélien Tchouaméni first aired. In clips that have been circulating online, Mbappé does not identify Mao by name. He says he "uses [the meme] with friends all the time".

The furore appeared to kick off on Monday night after Chinese football forum Dongqiudi drew attention to the comments in a statement, saying they were "inappropriate" and "hurt the feelings of Chinese people".

Screengrabs of the clip and meme have since spread quickly on Chinese social media, with people echoing this sentiment and even calling for a boycott of both the French striker and his club, Real Madrid.

But some have blurred the meme itself as well as the part of the comment they found offensive, when Mbappe refers to "a Chinese dictator".

Dongqiudi said in its statement that it was "unable to translate" his comments because they were "offensive to China and the Chinese people".

Many people are therefore also wondering what exactly Mbappe said and have responded to the angry posts and comments with questions, wanting to know more.

Weibo users are recirculating the clip by blurring the meme and redacting references to Mao

What is the reaction in China?

Chinese fans have been criticising Mbappé – who is popular in China and has huge brand endorsements – of "profiting from the Chinese market yet making remarks that offend the Chinese public".

"International public figures, in particular, should show greater respect and sensitivity, as national sentiment must never be taken lightly," reads another comment on Weibo.

As the anger online grew louder, Chinese brands began to cut ties, although they did not explicitly refer to the video.

The country's largest dairy producer, Mengniu, said it "firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any words or actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people".

Drinks giant Dongpeng issued a similar statement: "Our company firmly opposes and has a zero-tolerance policy towards any behaviour that offends national sentiments."

According to state-owned newspaper The Global Times, state broadcaster CCTV's news apps will not feature content related to the French striker. CCTV will also stop showing La Liga matches, Chinese media reported on Tuesday. Real Madrid is one of 20 clubs that play in the Spanish football league and is the most decorated team with 36 league titles.

China's foreign ministry has also weighed in, with spokesperson Lin Jian saying: "We have noted the relevant reports. Words and deeds that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

Mbappé has a significant commercial presence in China

China is a major market for international sports stars and homegrown brands have signed multimillion-dollar endorsement contracts with Mbappé, Norwegian striker Erling Haaland, and NBA player Stephen Curry.

By 14:00 local time on Tuesday, five of the top 10 trending topics on Weibo centered on Mbappé, with the hashtag "multiple brands terminate partnerships with Mbappé" topping the list.

"Don't ever come to China," read one of the top comments on Weibo.

Why is Mao a sensitive topic?

Mao founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled through tumultuous decades in the 1960s and 1970s.

His attempt at rapid industrialisation, which he called the Great Leap Forward, led to a famine that killed tens of millions. Then came the Cultural Revolution: a violent purge of anyone seen as a threat to Communism, which included Chinese intellectuals, landowners, artists and often rivals within the Party.

His death in 1976 brought a new era for China, which began to open its doors to the global economy. Even as the country moved away from Mao's rule, he continued to be hailed by the party as a national icon whose legacy was beyond reproach.

So jokes or memes about Mao are seen not just as an insult to the party but also its closely-guarded narrative about the country's past.

Mbappé has said some of the memes "reveal a lack of political and human awareness"

It's unclear when the Mbappé meme involving Mao began but his nickname, "the dictator", has made the striker the subject of many memes and jokes online.

Mbappé is widely regarded as one of the best footballers in the world and has wielded significant influence at the clubs he has played for. His extraordinary speed, goalscoring ability and worldwide popularity have made him a global icon, attracting millions of fans, major sponsorship deals and media attention, with his influence extending into fashion, culture and business.

In 2024, he sued a French influencer and kebab shop owner for using his name in the description of one of the shop's sandwiches, leading to more jokes about the nickname.

France teammate Ousmane Dembele jumped on the trend during the 2026 World Cup, calling Mbappé Mobut – a reference to Mobutu Sese Seko, the dictator who ruled the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire, for three decades.

In an interview with France Football in September, Mbappé acknowledged the light-heartedness behind many of these memes, but said they "sometimes reveal a lack of political and human awareness among people".

"There's a side that's a bit less funny, because we know the damage people like that have caused throughout history," he said.

"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions upon millions of people miserable... I don't think I've done that in my life."

stories.body:
The current global economic situation is confusing. On the one hand it’s characterised by inflation, and food and other critical supply shortages caused by the wars in Ukraine and the Gulf states. On the other, by optimism and economic growth caused by the boom in AI investments .

The situation both poses threats and offers opportunities to Africa.

On the upside, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank are predicting that African growth will be around 4.5% in 2026 and 2027. This is higher than the IMF’s estimates of 3.1% global growth in 2026 and 3.4% in 2027.

The IMF maintains that African countries are reaping the rewards of the painful macro-economic reforms that they undertook earlier in the century. The reforms are helping African governments weather the shocks caused by the wars in Ukraine and the Gulf.

But the World Bank has warned that 2027 African poverty levels will be higher than they were in 2022. UN Trade and Development (UNCTAD) reports that since 2010, the continent’s public debt has increased at about four times the rate at which its GDP has grown.

On top of this, the capacity of African governments to reduce poverty is declining. African governments spend an average 12% of government revenue servicing their debts. According to UNCTAD, this exceeds the amounts many African governments are spending on health or education. Furthermore, the director of the IMF’s Africa department has warned that African countries are likely to face increased food insecurity and rising inflation because of the combined effects of rising fertilizer prices and El Niño.

Evidence is also mounting that African countries will not be able to raise the US$4.1 trillion they will need by 2030 to meet their SDG goals and climate needs. Since 2010, African countries’ average external debt as a percentage of exports has doubled and is now equal to 140% of exports. The proportion of the debt owed to private creditors has increased substantially and is now about 45% of sub-Saharan Africa’s total debt. Moreover, Africa is often charged more for this financing than comparable countries in other regions.

This is happening at the same time as official development assistance – historically an important source of funding for Africa’s development projects and programmes – declined 24% in 2025 from the 2024 level and is expected to decline even further in 2026 and 2027. It is now at the 2015 level in real terms.

The legacy multilateral development banks like the World Bank and the African Development Bank are becoming an increasingly important source of finance for African countries. In fact, the World Bank is the single largest creditor to sub-Saharan Africa .

These institutions claim that they are working to increase the amount of financing they can provide. For example, the World Bank announced that its collaborations with the private sector leveraged US$35 billion in 2023 and US$112 billion in 2025. Funding for low-income countries is not growing as dramatically. In fact, the growth in World Bank financing to developing countries has only increased by about 1% per annum in real terms since 2000.

I have been working on international development finance and African development for over 30 years. It is clear to me that Africa is facing the most unpredictable and risky and the least friendly environment that it has faced in decades. However, Africans cannot afford to simply resign themselves to being hostages of fortune. Instead, they should take advantage of some of the opportunities that are being created by this confusing environment.

Here are six ways in which countries can do this.

The gaps

First, the continent needs to use its own internal resources more effectively.

Studies suggest that African pension funds, insurance companies and sovereign wealth funds hold a total of US$4 trillion in assets . But only a small proportion of these funds is invested in the continent. Efforts are being made to change this. For example, the recently established African Credit Rating Agency can play a role in promoting investments in African companies and in promoting the development of national and regional capital markets on the continent.

Read more: Africa’s new credit agency: why it’s needed

African governments can support this development by implementing their agreement to establish an African Financial Stability Mechanism . This mechanism would provide support to countries that experience financial crises. They can also take actions to reduce the loopholes that foreign and local investors can exploit to avoid paying taxes.

Second, African governments can make more effective use of the regional multilateral financial institutions that they have established. These entities, like the Afrexim Bank, the African Finance Corporation and the Trade and Development Bank, understand the African context well. They can be important partners for African development, particularly supporting economic and financial integration across the continent.

However, they do not always act as development banks. For example, AfreximBank sued South Sudan in English courts for the US$657 million that it was owed under its loan agreement. Other entities fought with Ghana and Zambia over their contributions to those countries’ debt restructurings. Their member states should provide clearer guidance on how these institutions can promote sustainable development and regional integration in Africa.

Third, the continent can establish an African chapter of the recently created borrowers’ platform . This initiative is designed to improve the bargaining position of sovereign borrowers in the global south. It can be a useful forum for sharing information, peer learning and capacity development relating to more effective government debt management. It can also help borrowers identify how to diversify the sources from whom and the currencies in which they borrow.

Fourth, African states can continue advocating for international tax reform. They have played a leading role in promoting and negotiating the UN tax treaty . This treaty, which is expected to be adopted and opened for signature in 2027, should help African countries raise their fair share of tax resources from foreign actors in their economies.

Fifth, there is the question of reparations for the crime of slavery. African countries like Ghana and states in the Caribbean have already raised this issue and its effects on Africa and the African diaspora in global forums. Earlier this year, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution declaring slavery to be the gravest crime against humanity. In 2027 the UK Privy Council will hear a case on the issue .

This suggests that there is space for Africa and its allies to think creatively about ways in which companies and individuals , in addition to governments, can support reparations.

Sixth, African states should increase their efforts to promote IMF reform. Already African voices have called for fairer and more representative governance and for more resources to be allocated on a concessional basis to low-income countries in crisis. Some voices also advocate that the IMF make better use of its gold reserves to fund its concessional financing facilities. The IMF currently has gold holdings worth about US$350 billion.

While there are legal constraints on its ability to sell this gold, with some creative thinking the IMF could make more active use of this dormant asset.

stories.body:
Africa’s move to cleaner energy could bring women new jobs, businesses and more control over their time. Solar and wind industries could offer paid work, while off-grid electricity and clean cooking could create openings for women to run their own businesses. Spending fewer hours collecting fuel and cooking could also free women to earn, study or build a business.

But none of this will happen automatically. The green economy could take off and women could still be shut out of the better-paid technical jobs, finance, contracts, business ownership and decision-making positions.

Cleaner technology does not automatically make society fairer. If new technologies enter societies where women already have less access to money, skills, assets and power, those inequalities can simply carry over into the new economy.

Read more: African women are key to fighting climate change – these are the green skills they will need

We are development economists who study how Africa can use the green transition to support social and economic development. In our new working paper , we looked at what needs to change in Ghana and South Africa so that instead of just receiving clean technologies like solar panels or electric stoves, women can have a real say in the policies, investments and business decisions of green industries.

We combined three types of evidence. We reviewed research on how energy affects women’s access to jobs and business opportunities. We examined how 14 major green-energy policies, six in Ghana and eight in South Africa, address gender inequality. These ranged from South Africa’s 1998 White Paper on Energy Policy to Ghana’s 2023 Integrated Power Sector Master Plan . Finally, we interviewed nine government officials, policy advisers, researchers and civil society specialists working on industry, energy and gender in both countries.

Read more: Green energy doesn’t benefit everyone: ubuntu ideas can help include more people

Our research found that in Ghana and South Africa, some policies address inequality between women and men; others barely mention it. Both countries lack reliable data, funding and staff with the skills to turn promises into action.

In South Africa, departments often work separately and treat gender inequality as someone else’s problem. Ghana has a national gender policy and dedicated ministry teams, but these often lack the staff and expertise to do the work.

For this reason, we developed the Gender-Transformative Industrial Policy framework. This is a practical way of designing green industrial policy so that it tackles the barriers, hidden biases and wider pressures that stop women from fully taking part in – and gaining from – the green economy.

Women get cleaner energy but miss out on well paid jobs

Our research found that in Ghana and South Africa, women are often concentrated in lower-paid and non-technical jobs. Men occupy most engineering, technical and leadership positions. This shows why skills matter: many of the best-paid green jobs require technical, engineering or digital skills, yet women remain underrepresented in these fields.

Our review also found that even improved electricity access can reproduce inequality. Men may use more electricity for productive commercial activities. Women continue to be most responsible for providing unpaid care and household work even if they get an electric stove and no longer need to cook on a fire. Giving a household electricity or a clean stove is therefore only part of the story. Who controls money, assets and decisions also matters.

Read more: Women are seen as ‘saviours’ or ‘victims’ in climate change debates: why this is a problem

Our review found that some policies in both countries recognise the time and effort women spend collecting fuel and cooking, their roles as workers and business owners, and the support they need. Ghana’s Renewable Energy Master Plan , for example, calls for better data on women’s participation, equal job opportunities and finance for women-owned businesses.

Other policies barely mention women. Even those that do often fail to turn promises into action.

The people we interviewed explained why. Women’s needs are often treated as an afterthought when governments plan energy projects, training, business funding and contracts.

How governments can offer more to women

We propose a Gender-Transformative Industrial Policy Framework. It’s based on the Triple B Framework developed by Gillian Marcelle to attract more investment, put money to better use and fund sustainable development.

Our framework is built around four issues: bottlenecks, blind spots, external influences and blended policymaking.

Bottlenecks are the practical barriers that hold women back. These could be limited access to finance, training, assets, contracts, transport and affordable childcare.

Blind spots are the hidden assumptions that make policies seem neutral while still excluding women. For example, training programmes that women cannot easily attend because of their location, timing or entry requirements.

Read more: Climate change and inequality are connected – policies need to reflect this

External influences recognise that donors, investors, development banks and civil society can attach conditions to funding and programmes that put women first.

Blended policymaking means energy policy cannot work alone. Progress depends on education, finance, labour, procurement, infrastructure and social policy working together.

Our framework therefore asks four simple questions:

what is blocking women?

what is being overlooked?

who is shaping the rules?

are policies working together?

These questions help turn the green transition into real jobs, businesses, ownership and economic power for women.

What needs to happen next

Governments can use our framework to check whether green energy policies will expand women’s economic opportunities or not.

Before approving a programme, governments should ask what could keep women out, whether its rules favour men, how funders affect who benefits, and what else needs to change so women can take part.

Read more: Solar power in rural Zimbabwe hasn’t reduced women’s unpaid work: can policy do better?

Women workers, entrepreneurs, engineers, community organisations and business groups should help design green technology programmes and set priorities.

Energy and industry ministries need clear responsibility and targets for women’s employment, business ownership and contracts, backed by budgets and better data. This means government departments must work together on:

education and training that expands women’s technical and digital skills.

green finance and public procurement programmes that help women-owned firms compete for investment and contracts.

labour and social policies to make workplaces safe and childcare affordable, and wipe out inequality in unpaid care.

There are many green technology opportunities for women in solar and wind jobs, and businesses in mini-grids, solar-home systems, clean-cooking services and battery-based solutions. These offer work in installation, maintenance, sales, finance and customer service.

Meaningful change means women becoming technicians, engineers, entrepreneurs, business owners and decision-makers, beyond mainly using green technologies.

stories.title: How Cleta Mitchell Turned Trump’s “Big Lie” Into a Movement
stories.summary: The post How Cleta Mitchell Turned Trump’s “Big Lie” Into a Movement appeared first on ProPublica .
