Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom

Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.

The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.

The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.

AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.

The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.

The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.

The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.

“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.

The US has banned humanoid robots from China , citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.

As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.

But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.

Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.

“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.

China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.

Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.

On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.

China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.

This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum , an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.

Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

A winged Chinese spacecraft bearing a strong resemblance to the US military’s X-37B spaceplane was photographed in orbit by a passing US-owned commercial satellite in 2024, and we finally have the image.

The Chinese spaceplane has delta wings, payload bay doors, a dark heat shield, and a rear-mounted service module with power-generating solar arrays. In other words, the design of the winged ship is, to a great degree, a copy of the X-37B spaceplane flown by the US Space Force.

The photo was taken by a commercial imaging satellite owned by a company called Vantor, known as Maxar in 2024. Vantor is one of several companies that provide reconnaissance imagery of locations around the world to the US military and US intelligence agencies. The same Earth-imaging satellites can point their telescopes at objects in space.

Lower-resolution views of a Chinese spaceplane showing the vehicle’s general shape were publicly available before the DIA assessment. A US Space Force official revealed Maxar’s observation at a 2024 conference in South Korea, but the Pentagon did not release the full-resolution image to the public until Monday, when it appeared in an unclassified Defense Intelligence Agency assessment of threats to the United States in space.

Catch and release

The DIA report doesn’t reveal much new about what the Chinese spaceplane does in orbit. China has launched four spaceplane missions since 2020, with durations of up to nine months. The fourth mission is in orbit today after launching in February. It is not publicly known whether China has one or more such spaceplanes in its inventory.

The Space Force has two X-37Bs flying in rotation, with the longest of their eight missions to date running two-and-a-half years from launch until landing. US officials have released photos of the X-37B vehicles, published information about their design and dimensions, and disclosed a handful of experiments they have carried into orbit. Most of the X-37B’s activities in space are classified.

Like the X-37B, China’s spaceplane lifts off inside the payload shroud of a conventional rocket, then operates as a satellite once in orbit. The spaceplane flies like a miniature unpiloted version of NASA’s Space Shuttle and reenters the atmosphere for an autonomous land runway landing at the end of each mission. Ground teams then refurbish it for another flight.

The “enhanced maneuverability” of spaceplanes makes them “more suitable for certain missions than traditional satellites,” the DIA said in its report. So far, the Chinese spaceplane has only flown in low-Earth orbit (LEO) at an altitude of a few hundred miles. One of the Space Force’s X-37B flights soared to an altitude of more than 24,000 miles before using aerobraking to set up for reentry and landing .

Spaceplanes like China’s and the X-37B can also deploy small satellites from their cargo bay. Most recently, China demonstrated an ability to catch an object in orbit, perhaps using a robotic arm. The vehicle now in space released a sub-satellite in June and recaptured it in July, then did the same thing again in August and September, according to an analysis of open source orbital tracking data by Jonathan McDowell , an astrophysicist who catalogs spaceflight activity.

A fleeting glance

The official name of the Chinese spaceplane is even a mystery. It is often called Shenlong in Western publications, citing reports from the 2000s about China’s development of a robotic spaceplane. Chinese state media only refer to the vehicle as Chongfu Shiyong Shiyan Hangtian Qi, or CSSHQ, which means reusable experimental spacecraft, according to a fact sheet published by the Secure World Foundation .

The DIA did not disclose the exact circumstances of Maxar’s observation of the Chinese spaceplane, such as its timing, location, or distance, but Earth observations often use cameras to view other objects in space as their orbits intersect, an emerging field known as non-Earth imaging (NEI).

NEI allows commercial operators and government analysts to inspect satellites. This is especially useful for gleaning information about classified or proprietary satellite designs, extending a new avenue for international and corporate espionage to the high frontier.

The capability exhibited by Maxar and other commercial companies in the NEI field is distinct from the recent actions of some military spacecraft, such as Russia’s Kosmos 2612, which deliberately maneuvered to approach a US-registered radar imaging satellite earlier this month. Commercial NEI observations come from chance encounters, often at extremely high speed.

Pew-pew with DEWs

The DIA’s assessment of space threats includes an update on China’s pursuit of anti-satellite technology, or “counterspace” weapons. The intelligence agency reported the Chinese military likely considers directed-energy weapons (DEWs) “ideal counterspace systems” because they can be used to permanently or temporarily disable a satellite. One potential use for lasers in space would be to dazzle a sensor on an adversary’s satellite.

“China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade, or damage satellites in LEO,” the DIA said. “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”

The DIA noted China’s testing of ground-based anti-satellite missiles and the country’s historic demonstration last year of satellite refueling in geosynchronous orbit, a regime some 22,000 miles (36,000 kilometers) over the equator, something no other country has achieved above LEO. China has also tested a robotic arm that could snag a spacecraft out of orbit, and now operates a growing fleet of satellites called TJS that routinely approach foreign spacecraft.

The US Space Force also has a constellation of inspector satellites in geosynchronous orbit and recently procured more that could be refueled, overcoming maneuverability limitations. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed last month that the Pentagon has fielded weapons in space , making the United States the first nation to acknowledge possession of orbital weapons.

Russia is pursuing its own orbital combat program, which includes an ambition to deploy a nuclear weapon in space, according to US intelligence officials.

A more conventional Russian weapons system, known as Nivelir, is designed to fire projectiles from one satellite to smash into another. The Russian military simulated an attack using the Nivelir system in 2020. In April, Russia launched a fleet of small satellites into an orbit close to a commercial radar remote sensing satellite owned by ICEYE that provides reconnaissance imagery to Ukraine. One of the Russian satellites moved within “tens of meters” of the ICEYE satellite earlier this month before backing away, US officials said.

stories.title: Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned
stories.summary: Plans to switch to digital landlines by January could leave remote areas of the UK vulnerable, MPs say.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 27 October 2026

Plans to switch off the UK's traditional landline phone network could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency, MPs have warned.

Landline operators aim to complete the switch to an internet-based network instead of copper-wire cables by the end of January next year.

The government and operators say the move to digital landlines will offer a more reliable service.

But MPs representing remote areas of the UK urged security minister Dan Jarvis to ensure that scrapping the copper-wire network did not make their communities more vulnerable in a storm or other emergency.

Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and continues to work in a power cut.

Labour MP Torcuil Crichton, who represents the Western Isles constituency of Na h-Eileanan an Iar, said: "Resilience is inbuilt in the islands but we have major problems with connectivity because of this move from analogue to digital phone lines."

He said that "when the power goes out people don't have the phone, they don't have the internet and often they don't have a mobile signal either".

Retail service providers have been giving back-up battery packs to vulnerable customers, which can keep landline phones operating for an hour or more.

But Crichton said this was "simply not adequate" and that mobile phone providers "simply don't have the means to maintain or keep their signal going during storms".

He urged the minister to get telecoms firms to "up their digital game" to protect places "on the edge where people are vulnerable, isolated from their neighbours, where the ambulance is an hour away and the storm is 70 miles an hour".

Similar concerns were raised by MPs from the West Country and the Lake District.

Markus Campbell-Savours, Labour MP for Penrith and Solway, said: "I ask the minister to imagine an elderly constituent living alone in an isolated Lake District valley where copper phone lines have been replaced by fibre.

"A storm takes out the power to their router in the night and by the time they wake, the modest battery back up has failed, as has the mobile mast, does the minister share my concerns that they would have no way to raise an alarm in an emergency and agree that we need a new technological solution to protect the elderly?"

'We won't be able to use our phones if we have a power cut' Published 22 December 2025

Switchover must protect most vulnerable - MPs Published 24 March 2025

Conservative MP Julian Lewis also raised concerns about the lack of a "back-up system" if digital phone services go down in the event of a cyber attack or other emergency.

He told Jarvis the copper-wire network "could have given us useful levels of resilience in an emergency".

Jarvis, who is spearheading the government's Be Ready campaign, which is advising people to stock up on supplies to be prepared for emergencies , said he would "look very closely" at the Tory MP's point.

He also assured West Country MPs that their concerns would be addressed at a government resilience summit, which was due to take place in Cornwall next month, and promised to raise concerns about telecoms firms with the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.

"Our telephone networks are a vital part of our critical national infrastructure and our emergency response in weather-related crisis supports the functioning of essential services and keeping people connected when they need it most," he told MPs.

The government says the switch to digital phone services is needed because the traditional analogue network is becoming increasingly unreliable.

Digital signals will be sent over copper telephone wires where they have not yet been replaced by fibre connections.

The government's Be Ready campaign advises people , external who have not yet "migrated to a modern digital network" to contact their landline provider.

"If you are a vulnerable customer, for example if you are a telecare user, your communication provider must provide a free back‑up battery unit," it adds.

More information is available on the government's digital switchover site , external .

stories.body:
Healey says people living in council tax A to D band homes to get £100 energy payment

Healey says people living in homes in council tax bands A to D will get a £100 energy payment this winter.

That will help 20m households, he says.

double quotation mark Let me say this to families at home. I know that with the conflict in the Middle East, rising energy bills are a real worry. I know that people look to government at times like this, not to solve all their problems, but to give them a bit of breathing space. So today I’m taking one further step this winter. For 20 million households in council tax bands A to D, I’m announcing a £100 energy payment for households.

OBR: 'It’s been a dismal period in British economic history'

The outlook for real household disposable income (RHDI) in the UK is “a pretty grim picture”, P rof David Miles of the OBR has warned.

[ Reminder: the OBR has cut its forecast for RHDI per person , and expects it will fall slightly in the near term.]

Speaking to reporters, Miles explains:

double quotation mark If you go back to just before Covid, and take that as your base, where we are now - seven years later, is virtually no growth in per person real household disposable income. That’s pretty unusual in the history of the UK.

To a substantial effect it is caused by higher energy costs, Miles explains, which the UK can’t avoid as it is a net energy importer.

Looking back over the last decade, Miles bemoans “it’s been a dismal period in British economic history.”

The Office for Budget Responsibility is running through its latest forecasts now, at a press briefing in London.

They are highlighting the “challenging fiscal background”, the tough economic forecasts for 2027, and the fact the UK is still on track to hit the fiscal rules – in the face of a lot of “upside and downside risks”.

UK bond yields falling as City welcomes 'dull budget'

John Healey appears to have achieved an important duty for chancellors on budget day – don’t crash the bond market!

UK bond prices are slightly higher today, which has pulled down the yield (effectively the cost of borrowing) on these gilts.

30-year bond yields, for example, are down 4 basis points (0.04 of a percentage point) at 5.698%. That pulls them further away from the 28-year high over 6% hit earlier this month.

The chancellor is being rewarded for a relatively quiet budget (despite the large number of measures).

Matthew Amis, investment director at asset manager Aberdeen, says:

double quotation mark “The gilt market wanted dull and they got exactly that. With oil and gas prices this high and with one eye on France, a dull budget is what was needed. All of the major obstacles presented to Chancellor Healey were avoided, as such gilts yields are slightly out-performing. Is this a gilt positive budget? Not particularly, but in the context of this year that is good enough. 2027 is going to present another fiscal challenge for Chancellor Healey, but today’s budget should provide enough to reassure gilt investors going into the final months of 2026.”

How budget contains record number of measures, but with almost none of them costing or raising £1bn or more

Most budgets have three or four big, headline measures – tax rises or tax cuts worth several billion pounds a year. As Sky’s Ed Conway reports , this budget was unusual, because it contained an unprecedented number of measures, but their average value was (in budget terms) minimal.

double quotation mark Two key snap charts on the Budget... 1) in sheer numbers of policies, it’s the “busiest” budget in modern history. 98 different scorecard measures(!) 2) BUT the average VALUE of those measures was the smallest on record. Every little helps? Or too much fiddling? Views may differ

Here are the two charts from Conway that illustrate this.

There is only one measure in the budget scorecard that will cost more than £1bn in 2026-27 (apart from extra money for the defence investment plan announced in June). That is the £100 household energy payment for people living in less expensive homes, which will cost £2.6bn.

It is also a budget that does not feature big tax rises. The increase that will attract the most media attention is the rise in the bank surcharge, but that only raises £305m this year, and £959m next year. The only tax rise in the budget that will raise more than £1bn a year is a reduction in the main rate for the writing-down allowance. It will raise just over £1bn a year by 2028-29.

OBR: tax burden to 'increase sharply' to record high

The OBR report says the tax burden is forecast to “increase sharply” to a record high. It says:

double quotation mark In the central forecast, total public sector receipts are projected to rise as a share of GDP from 40.1 per cent of GDP (£1.2 trillion) in 2025-26 to 42.9 per cent of GDP (£1.6 trillion) in 2031-32. Within this, as chart 4.1 shows, National Accounts taxes as a share of GDP (the ‘tax take’) are forecast to increase sharply from 36.0 per cent of GDP in 2025-26 to 37.9 per cent of GDP in 2027-28, surpassing the previous historical high, before then rising more gradually to reach a peak of 38.6 per cent of GDP at the end of the forecast period. This would be a 5.7 per cent of GDP increase on the pre-pandemic level of 32.9 per cent of GDP in 2019-20.

The OBR report confirms today’s Guardian story saying the Treasury estimates for future tax revenues are based on the assumption that the Rosebank oilfield will go ahead. (See 10.25am .) It says:

double quotation mark These forecasts [for oil and gas tax receipts] are based on the North Sea Transition Authority’s (NSTA) projection for total oil and gross gas production … This shows that production has been declining since the start of the 2000s and that this decline is expected to continue at around 10 per cent a year over 2027 to 2031. The projection includes production from currently producing fields (including Jackdaw), and the NSTA’s estimate of production from development of new fields, which includes Rosebank, and from future discoveries. The forecast annual pace of decline would be around 14 per cent a year if there were no production from any new fields.

The squeeze on mortgage-holders is going to get worse over the next few years.

The OBR has calculated that the average effective interest rate on the outstanding stock of mortgages will rise from 4% in 2026 to 5% in 2031.

That’s because mortgage rate have risen in line with the jump in government bond yields since the Iran war began, which will catch people who roll off mortgages that were fixed when rates were lower.

The OBR says:

double quotation mark …mortgage payments as a share of household disposable income are expected to rise to reach 4¼ per cent in 2031, the highest since 2009 and more than double the 2021 level of 2 per cent.

Mark Rutte, the head of Nato , has welcomed John Healey’s pledge to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030.

Posting on X, Rutte says:

double quotation mark Good news on the new budget from @JohnHealey_MP with a strong commitment on defence. The UK role in transatlantic security is vital, and I welcome this move to put 🇬🇧 on a credible path towards meeting the commitment made by all NATO Allies in The Hague - to ensure we’re all investing what’s needed to remain ready & able to deter aggression and defend our freedom and security

As covered earlier , Healey told MPs that next year’s spending review would set out details of how the UK will meet the target of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and 3% by 2030.

'Is that it?' - Badenoch ridicules budget, claiming big decisions postponed, and Healey should have cut welfare to fund defence

Here are some of the main points from Kemi Badneoch ’s response to the budget.

Badenoch dismissed the budget as minimal and underwhelming. People would think “its that it?” she said.

double quotation mark Most people in the country listening to his budget will be thinking to themselves, is that it? Really? Is that it? The prime minister came in promising to reverse 40 years of neoliberalism. Instead, we got 4p off gherkins.

She also said the budget did not “come close to meeting the moment”.

She criticised Healey for refusing to cut welfare to fund higher defence spending .

double quotation mark Unfortunately, just like every other Labour budget, the headline story is the same. More borrowing, more tax rises and surprise, surprise, more money on benefits … Next year, under Labour, the tax burden will be the highest in our country’s history. OK. And our benefits bill is going up by tens of billions of pounds because this government has put welfare first. We are overspent, over-borrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system. And this is his answer. It is simply not enough, not good enough, not strong enough, not bold enough … [Labour MPs] do not understand why it’s a problem that a quarter of all working-age adults are now claiming some form of benefits. They do not understand that if Russia launches an attack on Nato in the next three years, as the government’s own intelligence suggests, we will be at war without the means to properly defend ourselves.

She ridiculed Healey’s announcements on defence. (See 1.28pm and 1.30pm .) She said:

double quotation mark Yes, he has funded the defence investment plan – that is welcome. Yes, there is more support for Ukraine – that is welcome. But he said himself in June that wasn’t enough. What he’s done is he’s given himself a bit of breathing space until next year. Instead, what we have is a plan to have a plan. I bet Putin’s really scared now.

She welcomed Healey’s decision to ignore Labour MPs saying he should increase capital gains tax, his decision to pause equalisation of the younger people’s minimum wage with the full adult rate, and the U-turn on cash Isas.

She claimed the government was postponing tough decisions because Andy Burnham wants to keep open the option of an early election. She said:

double quotation mark We all know why he’s delayed until tomorrow, difficult decisions he should have taken today. It is because the prime minister wants to keep the option of an early general election.

She said she would not accept Healey’s invitation to support the 3% rise in the bank surcharge. (See 1.09pm. )

OBR forecasts no real earnings growth next year

Grim news for workers – the Office for Budget Responsibility is forecasting there will be no real earnings growth in the UK in 2027.

That means inflation will devour every crumb of pay rises the average worker wins next year.

It underlines how 2027 will be a tough year, with growth forecast to fall to just 1%.

The OBR then expects that real wage growth will then recover to around 0.5% a year by 2030, as energy prices drop back. But it warns that real wage growth won’t keep pace with output per worker, as firms will focus on rebuilding their profit margins.

Another blow – the OBR has also cut its forecast for growth in real household disposable income per person, a key measure of living standards.

It says:

double quotation mark Subdued real wage growth, alongside the combined effect of frozen income tax thresholds and higher nominal earnings growth, means we expect RHDI per person to fall slightly in the near term. RHDI per person then partially recovers as the energy price shock subsides.

OBR: probability of meeting the fiscal mandate has fallen to 56%

The OBR is warning that the government is slightly less likely to keep to its fiscal rules than a year ago.

The watchdog confirms that the fiscal mandate - for the current budget to be in surplus in 2029-30 – is on track, with a margin of £15bn (as John Healey told MPs earlier).

The OBR says:

double quotation mark This is £7bn lower than when the fiscal rules were last formally assessed at budget 2025. The probability of meeting the fiscal mandate is now estimated at 56 per cent, which compares to a probability of 59 per cent at budget 2025.

OBR: UK's challenging position has worsened since March

The Office for Budget Responsibility’s latest economic and fiscal outlook – the fiscal watchdog’s assessment of the budget – starts with a sobering warning that “the UK’s economic and fiscal position remains very challenging”.

The OBR cites the “repeated adverse shocks” that have led to weak growth and pushed up government borrowing.

Shocks since the 2008 global financial crisis. “including rising barriers to trade after EU exit, the pandemic, and the 2022 energy price spike”, it says.

And it warns that there have been “further adverse developments” since its March forecast, with both “interest rates and energy prices rising significantly”.

double quotation mark As a net importer of energy, the rise in energy prices constitutes a negative terms-of-trade shock for the UK, which pushes up on inflation and lowers real household disposable income.

This means the OBR now expects UK inflation to average 3.5% in 2027, up from 2% expected in March.

The Treasury’s budget documents are online here .

And here is the Office for Budget Responsibility’s economic and fiscal outlook report.

Gov.uk wobbles as public check out their council tax band

The government’s website seems to be creaking under the pressure as people check what council tax band they are in so they can see whether they qualify for the £100 support payment announced today .

You can check your tax band here: Check Council Tax Band .

But when we try, we get this error message:

Don’t all click at once….

Healey announces first-time buyer Isa

Healey ended by talking about housing.

He said, for people saving to buy a home, a first-time buyer Isa will replace the lifetime Isa.

He ended his speech saying:

double quotation mark The decision I’ve taken today will help steer Britain through and, when the storms pass, what matters is where Britain is heading – a Britain reindustrialised, a Britain with power returned to communities, threats deterred, global opportunities seized. In our first 100 days, this Labour government has set a course for fresh hope, good growth and support for those who need it. We know who we are. We know where we’re going. We can see the Britain we want. It’s a vision burnt into every line of this budget statement, breathing space now, fresh hope for the future, delivered to the British people by this Labour government.

stories.body:
British Retail Consortium says ‘dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs’ being kept from consumers

Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises for customers.

The lobby group said shop price inflation was 2.1% year on year in October, a sharp rise compared with 1.4% in September, and an indication that retailers were beginning to pass on the rising costs of energy and food ingredients since the Middle East conflict broke out.

It said food inflation, which has remained low during the past year, increased this month to 2.9% year on year – against a 2.5% rise in September – putting further pressure on the chancellor, John Healey, before his first budget on Wednesday.

Non-food inflation, which includes items such as clothing and footwear, more than doubled in October, from 0.8% to 1.7% year on year.

The price of Brent crude oil reached $117 a barrel in recent days, well above the $70 average in the months before the US and Israel attacked Iran in February. Gas prices have also risen sharply, pushing the UK consumer prices index to 3.5% last month .

Until this month, retailers had largely absorbed the higher costs of raw materials, mainly in response to weak demand from customers. In surveys, consumer confidence has declined sharply since the summer, when it became clearer the conflict in the Middle East was unlikely to end swiftly.

Bank of England officials are expected to raise interest rates next week from 3.75% to 4%. If the rise in retail prices persists, it is likely to persuade many of the Bank’s nine-member monetary policy committee to raise rates still further in December or the new year.

Helen Dickinson, the chief executive of the BRC, said: “The dam is starting to break on the huge wave of costs retailers have absorbed over the last two years.”

She said that while there was heavy discounting to attract shoppers ahead of Halloween celebrations, supermarkets could no longer keep the prices of tins and packets on their shelves from going up.

The chancellor is expected to come under intense pressure from his own backbenchers concerned that the high cost of living is harming many of their constituents.

The impact of cost of living pressures on low-income families is the subject of a report by Ruth Patrick, a professor in social and public policy at the University of Glasgow.

Based on a long-term study, it shows that high petrol and diesel prices are hitting families who need to transport disabled children to and from school and health appointments, and workers who use a car to travel to and from their jobs.

after newsletter promotion

Petrol prices above £1.75 a litre in many places and diesel often above £2 a litre can mean that work doesn’t pay, according to Patrick, who leads Changing Realities , an online project working in partnership with over 200 hundred families.

She said that in the last month almost three-quarters (73%) of participants surveyed for the project had shopped in the reduced-items aisle, while 62% had changed the food they buy and 63% had left the heating off even when cold.

One respondent, Rosie L, who lives in rural Scotland, said: “It’s getting to a point where I don’t know how we are going to keep managing to run our car.” She added: “Public transport is not accessible or reliable where we are [and] not having access to a car would affect every single aspect of our lives. Particularly as my children are disabled.”

The report involves responses from 76 participants, of which 73 shared strategies they had taken to reduce costs over the previous month.

Patrick said the help provided by governments and local authorities so far did not match the scale of the problem. “The budget provides an opportunity to make good on Andy Burnham’s pledge that his will be a ‘cost of living government’,” she argued.

“Taking sustainable and long-term steps to secure the adequacy of social security would be a vital step here, and there is particular scope in restoring the real value of child benefit, traditionally a vital source of support with the additional costs that come with children.”

stories.title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
stories.summary: Officials are expected to begin discussions on a range of options for the future UK-EU relationship before a summit next month.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds says no "assumptions" have been made about what the future UK-EU relationship could look like

Published 27 October 2026

British and European officials will discuss the future options for the UK's relationship with the EU, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds has told the BBC.

Officials on both sides are expected to begin discussions about a range of options, including free movement, before the EU summit on 20 November.

However, Downing Street has insisted the government's current focus is on achieving new deals in areas such as food and youth mobility at the summit.

Reynolds said no "assumptions" had been made about what the UK's future relationship with Brussels could look like.

Andy Burnham has said he wants an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and EU.

But the prime minister has been clear any major changes to the UK-EU relationship would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

He has vowed to stick by the red lines in Labour's 2024 manifesto, with no return to freedom of movement, the EU single market or customs union, for the duration of this parliamentary session, which will end by 2029.

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion Published 1 day ago

Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions in his next 100 days Published 1 day ago

Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement Published 2 days ago

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.

He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.

"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.

"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."

Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.

"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."

A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.

"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.

Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.

Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.

But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.

Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.

"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.

Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."

Speaking to BBC Wales, Labour MP Ruth Jones said: "We need to be very careful here. We must respect the Brexit referendum result."

Asked if a referendum on freedom of movement was something she would support, the MP for Newport West and Islwyn said: "We're a long way from that. Andy Burnham is floating the idea, and it's great to float ideas, but let's talk it through and see what does it mean, because another referendum at this particular time would be divisive."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.

On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.

The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.

But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times , external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.

The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

stories.summary: The Conservatives doubt whether women and girls will feel safer as a result of the funding.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 27 October 2026

Chancellor John Healey has pledged to give £15m to a fund established to tackle misogyny in schools, at work and in communities.

The government said the money will be provided over three years to schemes such as mentoring for young people, workplace training and communications campaigns designed to improve women and girls' safety.

Speaking on the eve of his first Budget, Healey said: "Every woman and girl deserves to feel safe, respected and able to pursue their ambitions - at school, at work and in their communities."

But Conservative shadow women and equalities minister Joy Morrissey said "not a single woman and girl is going to feel safer with this total waste of public money".

Swinney to introduce misogyny education in every school in Scotland Published 30 September

Women to advise mayor how to make London safer Published 4 September

Students face sexism and misogyny at weekend jobs Published 21 July

The "misogyny prevention fund" is expected to be confirmed in the Budget and is intended to support the work of a national taskforce established last month , external and chaired by Women and Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson.

Healey said the money will support "practical action to tackle misogyny head-on" and he hopes it will attract additional funding from businesses and philanthropists to increase its reach.

Phillipson said daily incidents of misogyny, including sexist slurs and workplace discrimination, have "no place in modern Britain".

She said: "This funding is a critical step as we work to confine misogyny to the history books, where it belongs."

Phillipson added that "everyone, from big business to members of the public, can do their bit to stamp out misogyny and improve the lives of women and girls everywhere".

When launching the taskforce chaired by Phillipson, the government said last month that it would aim to ensure government policy is "shaped by those most affected by misogyny".

It added its first meeting would focus on young people and later look at "workplaces, digital spaces and social cohesion".

Statistics published by the Office for National Statistics this month showed an estimated 12.8% of females aged 16 and over in England and Wales - around 3.2m - experienced at least one of domestic abuse, sexual victimisation or stalking in the year to March 2026.

The figure was an estimated 8.9% for males - around 2.1m.

For the Conservatives, Morrissey cited the estimates for women and girls as she criticised the announcement.

She said: "Labour simply aren't serious about tackling the crisis of violence against women and girls.

"This week it seems they will get the hard-pressed British taxpayer to fork out £15m to fund projects to tackle the 'manosphere'."

stories.body:
Tax policy means freezes reduce take-home pay as earnings rise in line with inflation

Income tax thresholds are set to remain frozen after John Healey’s first budget as chancellor.

One of the biggest tax rises in recent years has happened without a change in the rates at which people are taxed on their incomes. Instead it has come from successive government decisions to keep the thresholds associated with the tax at the same level each year, regardless of inflation.

Freezing tax thresholds results in “fiscal drag” – a phenomenon where people are dragged into higher tax bands when they get pay rises.

Until 2021, the UK income tax thresholds were typically increased each year in line with inflation. When the then chancellor, Rishi Sunak, delivered his budget that year he announced that thresholds would be frozen from April 2022 until 2026 .

The Conservative government extended that freeze until 2028, and last year the then Labour chancellor, Rachel Reeves , announced it would continue until 2030. Healey did not mention the freeze in his budget, but the documents show it remains in place.

You can use our tool to find out how much more tax you will pay over as a result of the freeze. We have used forecasts from the Institute for Fiscal Studies for inflation and applied them to earnings and thresholds.

The final figure is the amount by which your tax bill will effectively be larger in 2030, compared with what it would have been if thresholds had moved with inflation. In each intervening year the increase would be smaller, but similar.

Figures for earnings above £100,000 take into account the loss of some or all of the personal allowance.

Tax thresholds

These are the point where the tax rate on your income changes. In England, Wales and Northern Ireland the thresholds are the same.

Everyone has a personal allowance of £12,570, and below that income is not taxed. Income between £12,571 to £50,270 is taxed at the basic rate of 20% if it is on earnings. Income between £50,271 to £125,140 is charged at the higher rate of 40%, and anything over £125,140 is taxed at the additional rate of 45%. There are extra charges on savings and property income.

If you earn more than £100,000 once things such as pension contributions are taken into account, your personal allowance is reduced by £1 for every £2 you earn. By the time you earn £125,140 you will get no tax-free personal allowance.

It’s important to remember that it is only the income that is over a threshold that is taxed at that rate – if, for example, you earn £60,000, only £9,730 (£60,000 minus £50,270) is taxed at 40%.

Until 2021 the thresholds were typically increased in each year’s budget.

The impact of freezing

Many people get pay rises each year in line with inflation. When tax thresholds rise at the same time, this means more of their new earnings stay at the lower rate. When tax thresholds are frozen, pay rises spill over into the next bracket. As a result you may find that you take home less of your extra earnings than you expected.

The Office for Budget Responsibility says had the personal allowance moved up in line with CPI inflation since 2021 and until 2030-31, it would be £4,900 higher, with the threshold for the higher rate to kick in £20,100 higher.

It says the freezes mean the proportion of taxpayers paying either higher or additional rate tax will have increased from 15% in 2021-22 to 24% in 2030-31.

stories.title: Minimum wage set to rise but 18-20 year-olds will not get bigger increase
stories.summary: Chancellor John Healey will reveal the new pay rates in the Budget, and has also announced measures to help households with the cost of living.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 26 October 2026

The rise in the minimum wage is expected to be announced in the Budget, but 18-to-20 year-olds are set to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.

Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.

However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage.

Chancellor John Healey is also announcing measures to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living.

"The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time," Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the BBC:

"Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account."

The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from £10.85 an hour to around £11.27.

That is a smaller rise than the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place for younger workers since returning to power in 2024.

Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage for older workers, which is currently £12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to £13.20, the Times said.

Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job.

"Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally."

'Not going to change the world'

The government has also announced a number of measures, including removing import taxes on some food and ending the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments.

It says removing tariffs from 100 food items could save households up to £21 per year - or 40p a week - when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June.

"We're not going to say it is everything," Reynolds told the BBC, but taken alongside the changes implemented in the summer on goods such as pasta, fruit juice and tuna, he said it would save around £500m a year.

Other measures the government announced on Tuesday included:

Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that

Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead. However, this will not come in until 2030

Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to £194 a week for the period

And rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easier

Speaking to the BBC's Newscast, Healey said: "None of this is going to change the world. But if it helps around the margins and its action the government can take, then I want try and fix it."

The government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands. The 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since.

'I'm a single mum on £41,000 and limit my weekly shop to £40.' What do you want from the Budget? Published 3 hours ago

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 9 minutes ago

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds Published 2 days ago

The list of products the government is removing tariffs on includes:

Baked beans

Garlic

Gherkins

Chocolate-coated wafers and waffles

Boiled sweets

Toffees, caramels and similar sweets

Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes

Throat pastilles and cough drops

Plant-based drinks including soya, nut, cereal or seed

Kerosene

Fertilisers

The government said removing tariffs on fertiliser aimed to help farmers, while changes to import levies on kerosene is targeted at households that rely on heating oil.

The Treasury said it would publish on Wednesday a full list of the products that will have tariffs removed.

A tariff is an import duty paid by domestic businesses buying products from overseas.

Asked why the government was making it cheaper to buy goods from abroad rather than cutting business costs for UK firms, Reynolds said: "Where you can make a reduction in the cost of importing goods into the UK, when you think you can balance that with your domestic economic interests, that's a decision we will take."

But Balwinder Dhoot, director of sustainability and growth at the Food and Drink Federation (FDF), said: "It's more expensive to make food and drink here in the UK than in many of our close neighbours, as businesses face such high energy costs."

The Conservatives said the government's "everyday fixes" had already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Struggling households, new homebuyers and small shops stand to gain, while banks and online marketplaces could face higher levies

You be the chancellor: play our budget game to see if you can balance the books

John Healey will present his first budget on Wednesday, which will set the tone for Andy Burnham’s premiership.

Despite the chancellor’s promises in the summer that the tax and spending event would not be beset by the leaks that preceded those of his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, both official and unofficial sources have indicated much of what Healey is likely to announce. Here’s what to expect:

How much money is there?

Healey will allocate about £1.42tn this year on day-to-day spending and public investment. About £100bn of this will go on debt interest after a rise in the interest rate the government pays to multidecade highs .

Most of this increase can be blamed on the Gulf conflict launched by the US and Israel at the end of February, which has taken the oil price to above $110 a barrel and the price of gas to levels not seen since late 2022.

Government borrowing in this financial year has fallen compared with 2025-26, but not by as much as the Office for Budget Responsibility estimated in March, mainly owing to higher debt financing. Healey is spending about £1bn a month more than forecast.

Those costs mean the buffer of £24bn built up in the last tax-raising budget is likely to have halved to £12bn, according to the Resolution Foundation thinktank. The Treasury would be more comfortable having this headroom at about £15bn, according to economists at ING.

It’s a headache the chancellor could do without when he needs extra cash to fund cost of living measures, but also higher defence spending and the prime minister’s pet projects, such as devolution.

What does he want to spend money on?

The chancellor has promised to give consumers and businesses “breathing space” with a range of measures to help with soaring costs.

Everyday fixes: This is what the Treasury calls its proposals to help struggling households. They include an extension of parental pay to more than 150,000 additional parents per year worth £388, covering self-employed fathers and partners who have previously missed out.

Healey will also end the carer’s allowance cliff-edge , so unpaid carers no longer lose more than their allowance once they hit their weekly earnings limit. He will also remove import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, to reduce their shop prices.

Energy bills: The chancellor is planning to spend more than £1bn to help poorer households struggling with soaring gas and electricity bills, with the bulk going towards an expansion of the existing Warm Home Discount. An additional £100 could be added to this £150 means-tested yearly rebate, funded by taxes rather than billpayers as the current discount is.

Burnham has already suspended VAT on electricity bills for six months and on Wednesday morning Healey announced he was scrapping standing charges on gas bills in a move he claimed would save 60% of households on average £45 a year.

Help for first-time homebuyers : The budget will provide more detail of how the “your first home” scheme – first announced at Labour’s annual party conference last month – will work in practice. The revamped version of the Tories’ “help to buy” programme will give first-time buyers a 20% equity loan towards a new-build home, with an initial interest-free period and a minimum deposit of just 2.5%.

Defence: Healey aims to plug a £4.7bn gap in the government’s defence investment plan, inherited from Keir Starmer, with cuts to other departmental budgets ikely to be the main source of funding. However, despite resigning in June over raising defence spending to 3% of GDP, a roadmap showing how that target will be hit by 2030 will now not come until the spending review next year.

What taxes could Healey raise?

Healey is unable to increase rates of income tax, national insurance, and VAT without breaking manifesto commitments and has promised to stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules and not borrow to fund day-to-day spending. However, these are some of the revenue-raising measures he’s reportedly considering.

Bank tax: The Guardian revealed this month that the budget’s main revenue-raising measure is expected to be a levy on ​banks. The sector’s resistance has been undermined by a run of bumper quarterly profits on the back of higher interest rates, culminating in HSBC revealing on Tuesday that its had risen 32% to about £7.2bn .

Jeremy Hunt cut the bank surcharge – a supplement to corporation tax – from 8% to 3% ahead of the last election and one option on the table is reversing this cut to raise more than £2bn a year.

Taxes on online sellers: There has been strong lobbying from Labour backbenchers and unions to increase the taxes paid by online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay. The former Burnham adviser Andy Haldane used a Guardian interview to urge Healey to “level the playing field” with physical stores. One proposal reportedly drawn up would raise up to an extra £1bn by forcing them to collect VAT on behalf of large-scale sellers based in the UK as well as those overseas.

That money could be used to fund a cut in business rates paid by small high-street shops, possibly in the form of an increase to the threshold at which they start paying from £12,000 to £18,000. This would help the “bloody-minded entrepreneurs” that Healey has said he wants to support.

Other taxes: Alcohol duty is likely to rise in line with the retail prices index (RPI) measure of inflation, which will increase the tax on a pint from 50p to 52p.

What taxes is he expected not to touch?

Mansion tax: Treasury officials have played down speculation of significant changes to Reeves’s measure, which imposes an annual charge worth up to £7,500 on properties valued at more than £2m from April 2028. The chancellor was understood to be considering lowering the threshold to £1.5m, but London MPs have pushed back and are confident Healey has ruled out the move.

Capital gains tax : The chancellor has rejected calls by senior Labour MPs to raise CGT to the same levels as income tax. Some of his cabinet colleagues have called for the tax rates on income and asset gains to be equalised. However, influential figures, such as the former Treasury minister Jim O’Neill have pushed back, saying it would harm the incentives for wealth creators.

Fuel duty A longstanding freeze in fuel duty had already been extended to the end of the year , but it is due to rise by 3p a litre in January and 2p a litre in March. The default is also for an increase in line with RPI from April. However, with petrol and diesel at near-record highs the chancellor is expected to continue the freeze. Extending for an additional year could cost up to £2.7bn, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies, while keeping it to 2029-30 would cost another £4bn.

Inheritance tax: While the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch has proposed raising the tax-free threshold from £325,000 to £500,000 and excluding family homes from the calculation, Labour is not expected to propose any changes of its own.

Other measures

Devolution: Spreading decision-making to the far reaches of England is a major element of Burnham’s plans for economic growth. Healey will offer a £150m funding boost to help mayoralties and local authorities scale up for the new work they will carry out.

In addition there will be a £1.5bn borrowing facility. The package will also include the allocation of an initial £285m “good growth” funding next year, to be spent on local leaders’ priorities – which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.

Golden visas: Healey is understood to have scrapped plans for a new visa route to the UK aimed at wealthy people from overseas that were explored by the Treasury earlier in the year.

stories.title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
stories.summary: "We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night," the home secretary says while announcing the review.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Henry Nowak was 18 when he was stabbed to death in Southampton in December 2025

Published 26 October 2026

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.

The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.

Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust.

The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC.

"We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday.

Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.

In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.

Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said.

It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder. Chalk told Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that would include looking at whether any reports had been made but people or organisations had held back due to a "misplaced sense of cultural sensitivity".

Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene.

It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added.

The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.

The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.

The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice."

"We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement.

"Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review.

"There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.

The review is due to report in five months.

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: What CCTV tells us about how Henry Nowak's murder unfolded

Nowak, from Chafford Hundred in Essex, was a first-year accountancy and finance student at the University of Southampton when he was murdered.

On the night of Nowak's muder, it was Digwa's brother who called 999, claiming Vickrum had been attacked "racially".

Bodycam footage released by Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary, with the permission of Nowak's family, showed officers speaking to Digwa and others while Nowak lay on the ground.

Nowak could be heard repeatedly saying that he had been stabbed and could not breathe.

Violent disorder broke out in Southampton in the days following the release of the footage.

After Digwa's sentencing, Nowak's father Mark called for a "full, fearless and transparent" investigation into the police response.

But he also urged people not to use his son's death to "create further division, hatred or tension".

Critics warn of climate danger as president in Texas claims change will save companies and consumers billions

Donald Trump said his administration is “terminating” Biden-era regulations holding oil and gas companies accountable for large leaks of planet-warming methane during a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday evening.

“Tonight, I’m officially terminating Biden’s expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers,” Trump said, lifting what he called “crippling regulations on methane that caused prices to skyrocket” for small oil and gas operators. The change would save consumers and energy producers $45bn and unlock 210m barrels of oil, he said, which is equivalent to about 10 days of US petroleum consumption.

In a press release , the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator, Lee Zeldin, praised what he called Trump’s move “to end the war on oil and natural gas” by revising oil and natural gas regulations under the Clean Air Act. The proposal is expected to produce an estimated 210m additional barrels of oil and 1.41tn cubic ft of natural gas, according to the EPA.

The EPA’s proposal violates the Clean Air Act’s duty to protect public health and welfare and would seriously harm communities near oil and gas development, as well as the wider public, said Darin Schroeder, the methane legal and regulatory director at Clean Air Task Force (CATF). “EPA’s crusade against limits for emissions scientifically proven to harm public health and the environment must stop, and the agency must rescind this unlawful proposal and implement the 2024 rule without delay.”

Curbing pollution from the oil and gas industry is critical to protecting public health, said Harold Wimmer, president and CEO of the American Lung Association. “This not only carries environmental consequences, but leaks can also release harmful pollutants like volatile organic compounds that worsen air quality and carcinogens like benzene and formaldehyde,” he said. “If finalized, this proposal would help polluting industries avoid cleanup and harm the communities who bear the brunt of dirtier air and a warming planet.”

At a Trump rally in Corpus Christi earlier in the day, Trump shouted out Harold Hamm , saying the founder of Continental Resources was in the audience. In April, Continental Resources wrote a letter to the EPA pushing back against measures in the methane rule that prohibit routine flaring of associated gas.

Although some oil and gas executives spoke publicly in favor of the landmark methane rule , industry trade groups and corporations worked behind the scenes to gut the methane regulations, according to trade association materials and records obtained via the Freedom of Information Act by Fieldnotes , an oil and gas watchdog organization.

The 2024 methane rule required oil and gas operators to eliminate and minimize leaking, flaring and venting of methane and of volatile organic compounds, which are harmful to human health.

It was the first time the federal government had set nationwide requirements to limit methane emissions from existing oil and gas facilities. An earlier rule finalized under the Obama administration in 2016 applied to new and modified sources. Under the rule’s super emitter program , companies had to investigate major leaks near oil and gas facilities detected by third parties using EPA-approved remote sensing technology.

In March 2025, EPA administrator Lee Zeldin announced that the agency was reconsidering the Biden-Harris regulations “to ensure that they do not prevent America from unleashing energy dominance and continuing our trajectory as a leader in clean energy and emissions reductions”.

Last year, the US emitted more methane from its oil and gas sector than any other country in the world. Methane is responsible for at least a quarter of today’s warming.

Julia Kane, a researcher for Fieldnotes, said the Trump Environmental Protection Agency was giving oil and gas corporations exactly what they want. “The oil and gas industry says it’s a ‘good-faith’ partner eager to help craft regulations, but time and time again it’s worked behind the scenes to delay and weaken them,” she said.

Records obtained by Fieldnotes, including calendar events, presentation slides and meeting request forms, show that industry groups and companies met with the EPA to discuss methane regulations at least 38 times during the current administration’s first year.

“I do think it’s just an extraordinary level of access,” Kane said, adding that industry groups themselves were pleasantly surprised by their access under Trump. For example, during a conference call with industry representatives last year, Independent Petroleum Association of America executive Lee Fuller described a discussion with EPA staff, saying: “It was one of the more fascinating meetings that we’ve ever had, just because they were suddenly willing to talk to us. And they were also suddenly willing to talk about things that we’ve been trying to get them to do for years, and they’ve never even let it come on to the radar screen.”

Since the EPA announced it would no longer enforce oil and gas regulations in March 2025, oil and gas operators have leaked, vented or flared $7bn worth of natural gas , according to calculations by the Environmental Defense Fund.

Rosalie Winn, senior director and lead counsel at the Environmental Defense Fund, said the Trump administration was seeking to curtail the federal government’s ability to do anything to address climate pollution across all of the largest sectors responsible for emissions.

“What this administration is doing is enabling the worst polluters in the industry to continue to make ever more money off the back of American consumers while they’re wasting energy,” she said.

CPI release comes ahead of Reserve Bank decision next week as the Middle East conflict intensifies the cost-of-living crisis

Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s headline inflation rate has accelerated to 4.3%, with a key gauge that strips out volatile prices also elevated, sharpening expectations of another interest rate rise next week.

The Reserve Bank of Australia’s preferred measure of consumer prices, called underlying inflation, came in at an annual 3.6% to September.

RBA officials have strongly indicated the board may need to lift borrowing costs further to drag price growth back toward its 2.5% target, citing concerns of a “materially worse” inflation outlook .

The CPI release comes shortly ahead of the central bank’s next monetary policy decision on 3 November, when most economists are tipping another cash rate increase.

The RBA’s deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, described the inflation numbers as “too high” at Senate estimates on Wednesday, shortly after the data was released.

He said there was a “nightmare” risk that longer-term inflation expectations would pick up, making it harder to get inflation out of the system.

“We don’t think it is necessarily crystallising yet, but it is a particular risk,” Hauser said.

The cash rate, which informs lending rates including mortgages, already stands at 4.6%, its highest level in 15 years , after four rate hikes in 2026.

A fierce political debate has erupted in Australia over what is driving the cost-of-living squeeze, with critics pointing to a mix of high fuel prices caused by the Iran conflict, government spending and poor productivity.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said on Wednesday that while “we accept our part in the fight against inflation”, high oil prices and a recovering private sector were the main causes of the rise.

“The most important thing that can happen for Australians under pressure is to see an end to this war in the Middle East,” Chalmers said.

“This war in the Middle East has been disastrous for Australians, for cost of living and for inflation, right around the world.”

Growing unease

CPI figures released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday show that costs for everyday goods and services are rising at the same time as unemployment lifts , making life uncomfortable for households.

after newsletter promotion

Transport costs have risen 8.7% over the past 12 months, due in large part to escalating fuel prices stemming from the US and Israel conflict with Iran.

While higher fuel prices are trickling through the economy, there are price pressures everywhere.

Food prices have also jumped another 3.2% in a year, and housing costs were up 5.2%.

Stephen Smith, partner at Deloitte Access Economics , said the RBA had “little appetite to allow inflation expectations to drift higher after such a prolonged period above target”.

“The difficulty is that the economy is already slowing. Household spending is subdued, the labour market has softened and the housing market has weakened,” Smith, who is expecting a rate rise next week, said.

The escalating expenses have fed into the growing political unease in Australia and elsewhere, as voters express their discontent with cost-of-living pressures.

Housing, which is the single biggest category in the CPI, was the largest contributor to annual inflation, according to the ABS, followed by transport costs.

Builders have been passing on higher costs for materials and labour for new dwellings, while electricity prices are also elevated.

Josh Gilbert, market analyst at eToro, said inflation was turning into a “higher-for-longer” story in Australia.

“Anyone holding out for rate relief may need to pack plenty of patience, because another hike looks imminent after today,” Gilbert said.

stories.body:
The public accounts committee has said the risk to billpayers is ‘extraordinary’

The government’s plan to fund a multibillion-pound nuclear plant at the Sizewell site in Suffolk represents a “terrible deal” for the UK taxpayer over the rest of the century, according to the government’s spending watchdog.

MPs on the public accounts committee (PAC) have warned the government that the cost of the Sizewell C nuclear reactor could spiral to almost £48bn, leaving bill payers on the hook to provide an extra £9.8bn to construct the plant before 2040 and a further £12bn over its 60-year operating life.

Taxpayers and consumers face a “high level of risk”, according to PAC, after the government agreed to take a near-45% stake in the nuclear plant, which is considered a successor project to the heavily delayed Hinkley Point C nuclear plant in Somerset.

Under the terms of the multibillion-pound deal , which will be paid for through taxes and energy bills, the UK government holds a 44.9% stake while French state nuclear developer EDF has a 12.5% stake.

The rest of the funding has come from private investors including the British Gas owner Centrica, which holds a 15% share, alongside the Canadian investment group La Caisse, which holds 20%, and the investment manager Amber Infrastructure , which has a 7.6% stake.

The UK government was forced to take a larger than expected share of the project after buying out Chinese state nuclear developer CGN, which had been allowed to hold a 20% stake in Sizewell C before national security concerns emerged.

The watchdog warned that while the British public could be called on to shoulder multibillion-pound cost overruns, the nuclear project’s private investors would only need to put in an extra £30m.

Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, the PAC chair, said: “The high level of risk borne by taxpayers and consumers for the construction of Sizewell C is extraordinary. Private investors look set for significant returns on their investments, while customers are likely to be saddled with higher energy bills.”

He urged the government to “focus on the successful delivery of this project”, and in building confidence in the UK’s nuclear industry more broadly, so that taxpayers will “never be put in this position again”.

A government spokesperson said the report “completely ignores that investors are incentivised to complete construction as cheaply and quickly as possible” through the terms of the deal.

“Once operational, Sizewell C could save £2bn a year across the energy system, cutting costs for families up and down the country, and the project is already making good progress with over 2,000 workers on site,” the spokesperson added.

Sizewell C is projected to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn, with construction completing between 2039 and 2043. The committee has called on the government to provide the scenario analysis it used to underpin its cost estimates for the project within the next three months. It also asked ministers to provide an update on the project’s development every six months to keep track of its progress.

after newsletter promotion

Critics of the project, including Alison Downes of the Stop Sizewell C campaign group and Prof Steve Thomas of Greenwich Business School, who provided joint evidence to the committee, have suggested that the cost of abandoning the project today would be lower than the cost of paying inflated energy bills over 60 years “multiple times over”.

They called on the government to rule out using this funding model for future nuclear projects. “All it offers is a free ride for investors and financial pain for households,” they said in a joint statement.

Tom Greatrex, the chief executive of the Nuclear Industry Association, said Sizewell C would provide “clean, reliable and constantly available power” that could save households billions from paying the cost of balancing the grid or building extra network connections.

“Currently, the consumer is footing a bill of £2.8bn so far this year to manage a dysfunctional grid, paying both for wind to stop generating at some times, and for gas-powered backup at others,” he said.
